I just want to clarify something here. These PCR tests will probably be using either quantitative real time PCR (qPCR) or digital droplet PCR (ddPCR). qPCR is a very common laboratory technique that many, many people use, so this is a method that has been tried and tested. However, it must be interpreted in the context of all of its drawbacks as well. ddPCR is less commonly used because it's more expensive, but it is more accurate. Both these types of test are available for COVID-19. My guess is most people are using the qPCR method because it's a lot cheaper and far less accurate. The media does not tell you this. For this method, you first need to get the RNA you want to quantify. From a pharyngeal swab, this is going to be a really measly amount. You maybe get a tiny bit of cells, and those, if they have virus, a tiny bit of virus. You then need to convert this RNA into cDNA. Then, you take the cDNA and you do either qPCR or ddPCR. With ddPCR, the technique forms droplets so you can directly quantify the actual amount of a particular transcript you are looking for. With qPCR, it's far more complicated. To quantify it directly, you need to do serial dilutions and generate a standard curve against known concentrations of some transcript. Then you compare the signal from your fluorophore, which is a chemical that emits light detected by your qPCR machine. So do you have enough RNA from a pharyngeal swab to do serial dilutions? No fucking way. The other approach instead of serial dilutions is to use a control sample. So you have your test subject, who may or may not be COVID-19 positive. Then you have a sample that you know for sure, is negative. Then you compare them and look for the relative difference, and you have to decide, what relative fold change is positive? This is decided by taking known COVID-19 positive samples and seeing what the relative difference is, and you have to just set a cut-off. Inevitably, you will get some positive that are actually negative, and some negative that are actually positive. Now, in the typical lab setting, we are running 100 nanograms of genomic cDNA per sample. And we need to run them in biological triplicates! So that means, 3 independent samples. When you get your covid test, they take one swab. They cannot get 3 samples from that. For viral RNA, you don't need to get as much as 100 nanograms, but it's still going to be challenging to get enough RNA to do a robust test. Next, let's get into the primer design. You need flanking primers that are around 20 basepairs to amplify a sequence that is around 100-300 basepairs in length. For qPCR, there are 2 methods generally used. One is SYBR green, which uses just the two primers, and the other is TaqMan, which uses the 2 primers and also a 3rd probe that binds to the final transcript. TaqMan is more accurate and is typically what is used for diagnostic assays. With just the 2 primers, you can get a off-target effects, but having the 3rd probe for Taqman-based assays really increases your specificity, so it's a fairly robust in this aspect. Now let's talk about the cycle numbers. For qPCR, it will generally run for around 40 cycles, and it sets a threshold for the signal. Once the signal gets large enough, it records a "cycle number". The more of your target you have, the faster it will get a high signal, so the lower the cycle number will be. If you have absolutely nothing, the signal should remain at 0 no matter how many signals you run. However, if you have a little bit in there, you can run it for many, many cycles, and eventually you will get something. Is this positive? It's hard to say because you just got a tiny bit of RNA from a pharyngeal swab. Also, do we know if this target is specific to COVID-19 or if it can also be positive for other viruses? It's possible. Also, there is the issue of interpreting the result. If there is a positive PCR result, does that mean there are cells infected with COVID-19 that are actively producing virus or could it be COVID-19 on the pharyngeal surface that has been destroyed by the body and the person is not infected? The test doesn't tell us that. In a laboratory setting, if you have a cycle number at 25, that is considered fairly abundant, but a cycle number at 40 basically means you have nothing. You have to think of these on the scale of a power of 2. Each PCR cycle doubles the amount of the target transcript. So 25 cycles means you've duplicated the original amount by 2^25 times. 40 cycles means you've duplicated the original amount by 2^40 times. Okay, now let's talk about "housekeeping genes". You can't just run the test on your covid-19 target, you also need to run it on a "housekeeping gene" in order to normalize your sample. Even in the research setting, we know that these "housekeeping genes" we use for normalization are not always reliable either. They likely would have to normalize it so we know the number of viral particles PER cell. if you don't normalize, you have no idea if you have more virus because you got more cells or if you have a lot of virus in each cell. Of course, if you have active infection and the cells are producing a lot of virus, you will get more virus per cell. On the other hand, if you got exposed but you managed to kill off the virus, it could still potentially on the swab but you won't get a huge number of particles per cell. The media portrays these tests as "gold standard" but COVID-19 is new, there is no gold standard. There are so many types of tests available that none of them are comparable. I guarantee different companies even use different primers in their tests. You're going to see a lot of variability in terms of how reliable some tests are. Even in the laboratory setting where we use these assays very often, we understand that they have strengths and weaknesses, and the key is reproducibility. I've run qPCR on the same sample, using the same primers, reagents, machine, but on different days, and have gotten vastly different results. Finally, these tests should never be interpreted in isolation. They should and must always be interpreted in a clinical context, meaning you have to look at it in combination with the clinical picture. If you have someone with all the symptoms of COVID and you do this test, this tells you, with some certainty that he person has covid. However, if you are just testing everyone for no good reason, you will get a lot of false positives. This is an issue of statistics that needs its own really huge explanation, including concepts like sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, etc. However, essentially, it's helpful if you are testing covid in a population of people that all have covid symptoms, but stupid if you are testing random people in the population with no symptoms.

TLDR. PCR testing uses adjustable sensitivity. The higher the sensitivity the greater the false positive match to your target. Dialed up high enough you get 100% positive results to any sample. PCR tests are borderline worthless for anything around 35.
